Simulate the Banister impulse-response model

Source: R/banister.R
simulate_banister.Rd

Computes fitness, fatigue and predicted performance for every day of a daily training-load series, within each athlete, from parameters given by the user (MODELS.md, M-01 to M-03). Nothing is fitted: this version only simulates.

Usage

simulate_banister(
  x,
  k1,
  tau1,
  k2 = NULL,
  tau2 = NULL,
  p0 = 0,
  model = c("two_component", "fitness_only"),
  same_day_load = c("exclude", "include"),
  initial_fitness = 0,
  initial_fatigue = 0,
  missing_load = c("error", "zero")
)

Arguments

x

A daily_load object, from as_daily_load(). It is checked first; an object changed after it was built (for example by subsetting) must be rebuilt with as_daily_load().

k1

Gain of fitness, a single finite number >= 0.

tau1

Time constant of fitness in days, a single finite number > 0. Arguments are time constants, never half-lives (D-024): see time_constant() to convert a half-life.

k2

Gain of fatigue, a single finite number >= 0. Required for the two-component model; must not be given for the fitness-only model.

tau2

Time constant of fatigue in days, a single finite number > 0. Required for the two-component model; must not be given for the fitness-only model.

p0

Baseline performance, a single finite number.

model

"two_component" (the default; fitness and fatigue) or "fitness_only" (D-023).

same_day_load

Timing convention: "exclude" (the default) or "include". See the section on the timing convention.

initial_fitness, initial_fatigue

Fitness and fatigue on day 0, single finite numbers >= 0. The fitness-only model has no fatigue, so initial_fatigue must be 0.

missing_load

What to do with missing loads: "error" (the default) or "zero" to count them as load 0.

Value

An object of class c("banister_sim", "data.frame") with one row per row of x, in the same order, and the columns athlete, date, load, fitness, fatigue (NA for the fitness-only model), predicted and, if x has a performance column, observed. The attributes model, same_day_load, parameters (named numeric vector) and initial_state record the arguments used. Its print method shows them, with the half-life of each time constant.

Formula

Fitness \(g\) and fatigue \(h\) are exponential filters of the daily load \(w\) with time constants \(\tau_1\) and \(\tau_2\) (MODELS.md, M-01). The two-component model (M-02) predicts $$p(t) = p_0 + k_1\,g(t) - k_2\,h(t),$$ and the fitness-only model (M-03) predicts $$p(t) = p_0 + k_1\,g(t).$$ The columns fitness and fatigue are \(g\) and \(h\) without their gains. They are computed in recursive form.

Timing convention and default

  • same_day_load = "exclude" (the default; Busso & Chalencon 2023): the load of day \(t\) affects performance from day \(t + 1\), $$g(t) = [g(t-1) + w(t-1)]\,e^{-1/\tau}.$$ This corresponds to a performance test done before that day's training.

  • same_day_load = "include" (Morton et al. 1990, Eqs. 4-5): the load of day \(t\) counts on day \(t\) at full weight, $$g(t) = g(t-1)\,e^{-1/\tau} + w(t).$$

The two conventions give different numbers: gains obtained under one are not comparable with the other. The default "exclude" (DECISIONS.md, D-012) differs from the default of the load descriptors such as rolling_load(), which is "include" (D-021).

Initial state

Fitness and fatigue start from initial_fitness and initial_fatigue on day 0, both 0 by default (D-025). An initial value \(g_0\) adds \(g_0\,e^{-t/\tau}\) to day \(t\) under both conventions (MODELS.md, M-01). Each athlete starts from the same initial state on their first day.

Missing loads

Missing loads are never replaced silently (D-016). By default a series with a missing load is an error that names the first missing day. With missing_load = "zero" missing loads count as load 0 and a message says how many; the load column of the result still shows them as NA.

References

Morton RH, Fitz-Clarke JR, Banister EW (1990). Modeling human performance in running. Journal of Applied Physiology, 69(3), 1171-1177.

Busso T, Chalencon S (2023). Validity and accuracy of impulse-response models for modeling and predicting training effects on performance of swimmers. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, 55(7), 1274-1285.

Marchal A, Benazieb O, Weldegebriel Y, Méline T, Imbach F (2025). Statistical flaws of the fitness-fatigue sports performance prediction model. Scientific Reports, 15, 3706.

See also

session_response() for the response to a single session, constant_training() for constant daily training, half_life(), as_daily_load(). The article "The Banister model" on the package website discusses the limitations of the model.

Examples

# Morton et al. (1990): load 100 on days 1-60, then 60 days of rest
x <- as_daily_load(
  data.frame(date = as.Date("2026-01-01") + 0:119,
             load = c(rep(100, 60), rep(0, 60))),
  date = "date", load = "load"
)
sim <- simulate_banister(x, k1 = 1, tau1 = 45, k2 = 2, tau2 = 15,
                         same_day_load = "include")
sim
#> <banister_sim> Banister model simulation: two-component model
#> Timing convention: same_day_load = "include" (a day's load counts on the same day)
#> Parameters: p0 = 0, k1 = 1, k2 = 2
#> Time constants: tau1 = 45 days (half-life 31.19 days), tau2 = 15 days (half-life 10.4 days)
#> Initial state: fitness 0, fatigue 0
#> Nothing is fitted: values are simulated from the parameters given.
#> 
#>    athlete       date load  fitness  fatigue predicted
#> 1        1 2026-01-01  100 100.0000 100.0000 -100.0000
#> 2        1 2026-01-02  100 197.8023 193.5507 -189.2991
#> 3        1 2026-01-03  100 293.4552 281.0680 -268.6809
#> 4        1 2026-01-04  100 387.0059 362.9411 -338.8764
#> 5        1 2026-01-05  100 478.5006 439.5339 -400.5673

#> 7        1 2026-01-07  100 655.5018 578.2191 -500.9363

#> 10       1 2026-01-10  100 906.6817 754.4738 -602.2658
#> # ... 110 more rows
which.min(sim$predicted)
#> [1] 16

# Fitness-only model, default convention "exclude"
simulate_banister(x, k1 = 1, tau1 = 45, model = "fitness_only")
